questions.html:
Which of the following is/are valid assignment(s) of the pointer for the given declaration? An assignment is valid if both pointers are of the same type (pointers are compatible) and get successfully compiled with no warning or error.

int a[5]= {1,2};
int (*p)[5];

options.html: p = a;
p = &a;
p = *a;
p = **a;

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 39)

Option A: p=a; → Here a is a pointer to first element of array. P is a pointer to an array of 5 elements.

Option B: p=&a; : &a is a pointer to whole array of 5 elements and p is also a pointer to array of 5 elements . so it is a valid statement.

Option C: p=*a; P is a pointer to whole array & *a is accessing first element of the array.

Option D: p=**a; : **a is not a legal statement since *a means that its accessing first element of array and **a does not mean anything. So it is not a valid statement.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Given the declaration int a[5] = {1, 2}; and int (*p)[5];, the valid assignment is p = &a;.

Here is an analysis of each assignment and a conceptual diagram:

1. p = a;

  • Invalid. a decays to a pointer to its first element, which is of type int*. However, p is a pointer to an array of 5 integers (int (*)[5]). These types are incompatible.

Code

+---+---+---+---+---+
| 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |  <-- Array 'a' (int[5])
+---+---+---+---+---+
  ^
  | (Type: int*)
  |
  |  (Incompatible with int (*)[5])
  |
  p (Type: int (*)[5])

2. p = &a;

  • Valid. &a represents the address of the entire array a. The type of &a is int (*)[5], which perfectly matches the type of p.

Code

+---+---+---+---+---+
| 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |  <-- Array 'a' (int[5])
+---+---+---+---+---+
^
| (Type: int (*)[5])
|
p (Type: int (*)[5])

3. p = *a;

  • Invalid. *a is equivalent to a[0], which is an int value (in this case, 1). You cannot assign an int value to a pointer.

Code

+---+---+---+---+---+
| 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |  <-- Array 'a' (int[5])
+---+---+---+---+---+
  ^
  | (Value: 1, Type: int)
  |
  |  (Incompatible with int (*)[5])
  |
  p (Type: int (*)[5])

4. p = **a;

  • Invalid. **a is equivalent to *(a[0]). This attempts to dereference an int value, which is an invalid operation and would result in a compilation error.

Code

+---+---+---+---+---+
| 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |  <-- Array 'a' (int[5])
+---+---+---+---+---+
  ^
  | (Value: 1, Type: int)
  |
  |  (Attempting to dereference an int is invalid)
  |
  p (Type: int (*)[5])

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Given:

 
int a[5] = {1,2};
int (*p)[5];

Let's determine the type of each expression:

  • a → in most expressions, an array decays to a pointer to its first element, so a has type int *.
  • &a → address of the whole array, type int (*)[5].
  • *a → first element of the array, type int.
  • **a → invalid (*a is already an int, not a pointer).

Since p is declared as:

 
int (*p)[5];

p must be assigned a value of type int (*)[5] (pointer to an array of 5 integers).

Options

A.

 
p = a;

a is int *, not int (*)[5] 

B.

 
p = &a;

&a is int (*)[5], exactly matching p 

C.

 
p = *a;

*a is int 

D.

 
p = **a;

**a is invalid because *a is an int 

Correct Answer

B. p = &a; 

Source solution 4 (score: 0)


a (Option A): Points strictly to the first element cell (a). Type is int*. This does not match p.

&a (Option B): Points to the entire block container holding all 5 items. Type is int (*)[5]. This matches p perfectly.

*a (Option C): Pulls out the integer value 1 directly inside the first cell. An integer cannot be assigned to a pointer variable.

 

TRICK to find a pointer's exact type:

  •  check where pointer + 1 points; once you know the size of that jump, you know the type.

questions.html:
Which of the following is NOT a valid C program? A valid program is a program having no compile-time errors.

Program 1
auto int a; 
main ()
{
  auto int b; 
  for (b = 0; b < 10; b++)
  {
    auto int a = b; 
  }
}

Program 2
static int a; 
main ()
{
  static int b; 
  for (b = 0; b < 10; b++)
  {
    static int a = 1; 
  }
}

Program 3
int a; 
main ()
{
  static int b; 
  for (b = 0; b < 10; b++)
  {
    static int a = 1; 
  }
}

Program 4
extern int a; 
main ()
{
  static int b; 
  for (b = 0; b < 10; b++)
  {
    static int a = 1; 
  }
}
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 20)

In program 1, during compilation compiler sees auto int a; as a global variable and in auto int a we can say that we cannot declare auto int as a global variable since auto storage class is only used for variables which are defined locally and auto is not defined locally in this case.

In program 2, a is a static variable and we can define static globally and locally. We defined static variable b inside the main function and then we have for loop in which we have defined another variable of static storage class which in every iteration adds local a and upper block’s b to it.

In program 3, a is a global variable . We defined static variable b inside the main function and then we have for loop in which we have defined another variable of static storage class which in every iteration adds local a and upper block’s b to it.

In program 4, extern a is a reference to some variable a which is present somewhere else in this file or another file. We defined static variable b inside the main function and then we have for loop in which we have defined another variable of static storage class which in every iteration adds local a and upper block’s b to it.

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

Program 1 is not a valid program in C.
Option A is correct.
auto variables should always be within a block.
So program 1 will have “compiler error” as scope checking is done by the compiler. Therefore during compilation when the compiler encounters an auto variable that is supposed to be inside a  block but is present outside a block (global declaration), it will show an error.

In prog 4, there is no linker error. Because we are not even using the ‘a’ referred by the extern. Actually,
inside the for loop, the static ‘a’ is being used.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Answer: Program 1 will throw error


REASON

Program 1 :- "auto" storage class can only be used as local variable
The question arises why ??
The reason the variables declared as Auto gets stored in the stack area  whereas Global variable stored in static area so there is conflict for the compiler between the two storage classes

Program 2 :- No error 
Because one is "a" has a global scope whereas the a inside the for loop has a local scope it will overwrite everytime "a" is used in its block 

Program 3 :- No error 
Because one is "a" has a global scope whereas the a inside the for loop has a local scope it will overwrite everytime "a" is used in its block 

Program 4 :- No Compiler Error, No linker Error 
Question arises why ??
So the extern class tells the compiler that there is a global variable named "a" in this file or another file, also extern is kind of declaration it doesnot allocate memory
now when the compiler goes line by line (compiler reads from line 1, execution of code starts from main) and encounters static int a=1 you may say "that okay there is a variable "a" and is locally defined but the compiler expects "a" to be global variable so there will be a compiler error", but wait this is not the case as static int a=1 just overwrites or shadows the global "a" and hence no error
and since global "a" is not used anywhere so no linking error as well 

consider the code below:

int main(){
    extern int i;
    int i =10;
    printf(i);
    return 0;
}

This code will throw a compiler error because at one place you say there is a "GLOBAL" variable i and in the next line you go on declaring a local variable "i" inside the local scope.

questions.html: Which of the following is/are TRUE about storage classes in C programming

options.html: static local variables are NOT available to the linker.
static global variables are available to the linker.
extern local variables are available to the linker.
extern global variables are NOT available to the linker.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Answer: A, C

A: True, local variables anyhow are not available to the outer scope in current file, let alone to the linker

B: False, Static variables are never available to the linker.

C: True, extern local variables are just declaration which ought to be defined somewhere else, either in same file (outer scope) or in another.

D: False, Even if global, extern is just a declaration, the actual definition of variable (or function) can be somewhere else so it is natural that it in fact IS available to the linker.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Key facts

  • static local variable
    • Has block scope and no linkage.
    • Exists for the entire program execution, but its name is not visible outside the block.
    • Therefore, it is not available to the linker.
  • static global variable
    • Has internal linkage.
    • Visible only within the same source file.
    • Not accessible from other translation units.
    • Therefore, not available to the linker for external linking.
  • extern global variable
    • Has external linkage.
    • Can be referenced from other source files.
    • Therefore, available to the linker.

  • extern local declaration

     
    void f() {
    extern int x;
}

    This is merely a declaration of an externally linked global variable within a block. The variable x itself has external linkage and is resolved by the linker.

    • Therefore, it is available to the linker.

Evaluate the options

A. static local variables are NOT available to the linker.
True

B. static global variables are available to the linker.
False (they have internal linkage)

C. extern local variables are available to the linker.
True (the declaration refers to an externally linked object)

D. extern global variables are NOT available to the linker.
False (they are specifically meant for external linkage)

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

 

Answer: $A,C$

questions.html: The default storage class for functions in C language is –
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 14)

The default storage class for functions in C language is extern because functions themselves are always external and C language does not allow functions to be defined inside other functions.

Option – C

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

In C programming, the default storage class for functions is extern. This means that by default, a function is visible to the entire program (including other files), unless it is explicitly defined with the static keyword to restrict its scope to the file in which it is defined.

  • Extern : Functions are globally accessible across different files in a project by default.
  • Static : If applied to a function, it limits the function's scope to the file where it is declared.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

The correct answer is C. Extern

Quick Facts:

  • By default, every function declared or defined in C has a global scope and visibility across all source files.
  • This means the compiler implicitly adds the extern keyword if you don't specify any storage class.
  • If you want to restrict a function's visibility to only the current file, you must explicitly declare it as static
  • The auto keyword can only be applied to local variables inside functions, not to functions themselves.

questions.html:
Consider the following declaration of struct.

struct myst{
    char a[20];
    char *b;
    struct myst *p;
}x[2] = {"GATE", "Overflow", x+1, "GO", "Classes", x}, *p = x;

What will be the output of the following print statement?

printf("%s", p++->p->b++);
questions.solution:
Answer: B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

Answer: B

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_point#Sequence_points_in_C_and_C++

Before a function is entered in a function call. The order in which the arguments are evaluated is not specified, but this sequence point means that all of their side effects are complete before the function is entered. In the expression f(i++) + g(j++) + h(k++), f is called with a parameter of the original value of i, but i is incremented before entering the body of f. Similarly, j and k are updated before entering g and h respectively. However, it is not specified in which order f(), g(), h() are executed, nor in which order i, j, k are incremented. If the body of f accesses the variables j and k, it might find both, neither, or just one of them to have been incremented. (The function call f(a,b,c) is not a use of the comma operator; the order of evaluation for a, b, and c is unspecified.)

The operators ++, → have same precedence so the associativity will come into the picture, L → R in this case.

Again let’s change some variables name to avoid confusion.

    struct myst{
    char a[20];
    char *b;
    struct myst *p;
    }x[2] = {"GATE", "Overflow", x+1, "GO", "Classes", x}, *ptr = x;
    printf("%s", ptr++->p->b++);

‘p’ is a member(child) variable and can not be accessed without accessing it’s parent (x[0], x[1] in this case)(I don’t think C has parent child terminology I used that just for understanding).

The original value ‘ptr’ will be used and incremented later.

ptr → p is effectively same as saying x[0].p which is a pointer to the second (1-th) element of x.

ptr → p → b is the pointer to string literal “Classes” .

 

Side effects:

ptr = ptr + 1 * sizeof(*ptr). which is the address of “x+1”. ptr now is pointing to the second (1-th) element of the array.

b = b + 1 * sizeof(b*): that now is pointing to the first element/base address of “lasses”.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

 

Correct Answer: B. Classes

To understand the output, we need to break down the initialization of the structures and then trace the execution of the printf statement.

1. Analyzing the Memory Initialization

The code defines an array x of size 2, containing struct myst elements.

  • struct myst definition:

    • a[20]: a character array.

    • *b: a character pointer (string).

    • *p: a pointer to a struct myst.

  • Initialization of x[0]: {"GATE", "Overflow", x+1}

    • x[0].a = "GATE"

    • x[0].b = "Overflow"

    • x[0].p = x + 1 (This points to the second element, x[1]).

  • Initialization of x[1]: {"GO", "Classes", x}

    • x[1].a = "GO"

    • x[1].b = "Classes"

    • x[1].p = x (This points to the first element, x[0]).

  • Pointer p: Initialized to point to x (which is &x[0]).

2. Analyzing the Expression: p++->p->b++

This expression involves pointer arithmetic and structure dereferencing. We must follow operator precedence and associativity. The operators -> and ++ (postfix) have the same precedence and associate from left to right.

The expression is effectively parsed as: ( (p++) -> p ) -> b++

Let's evaluate it step-by-step:

  1. p++:

    • This is a post-increment. It uses the current value of p for this part of the expression and increments p afterwards.

    • Value used: Pointer to x[0].

    • Side effect: p now points to x[1].

  2. ...->p:

    • We follow the pointer returned in step 1 (x[0]) to access its member p.

    • From our initialization, x[0].p points to x[1].

    • Value: Pointer to x[1].

  3. ...->b:

    • We follow the pointer from step 2 (x[1]) to access its member b.

    • From our initialization, x[1].b points to the string "Classes".

    • Value: Pointer to the string "Classes".

  4. ...b++:

    • This is a post-increment on the pointer to the string.

    • Value used: The current value of the pointer is returned. The current value points to the start of "Classes".

    • Side effect: The member b in x[1] is incremented to point to the next character ('l'), so effectively it now points to "lasses".

3. Final Output

The printf("%s", ...) function receives the value returned by Step 4, which is the pointer to the string "Classes".

Therefore, the output is Classes.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Overflow: This would be the output if the expression accessed x[0].b. This would require p to point to x[1] initially or for the logic to circle back to x[0], which it does not.

  • C. verflow: Similar to A, but with an incremented pointer.

  • D. lasses: This would be the output if the increment on b was a prefix increment (++b), which would return the new value instead of the old one.

questions.html:
Which of the following function declaration can be passed to the following array?

char myArray[3][4];

options.html: void fun(char a[][], int size);
void fun(char a[][4], int size);
void fun(char [3][], int size);
void fun(char [][]a, int size);

questions.solution:
Answer: B, D, A

Source solution 1 (score: 14)

Answer: B

There are 3 ways to pass 2D array to a function.

void fun(char (*a)[4], int size);

void fun(char a[][4], int size);

void fun(char a[3][4], int size);

Internally compiler will always convert it to 

void fun(char (*a)[4], int size);

PS: We are not passing entire 2D array to the function we are passing pointer to the 1D array of size 4.

(Source: C Programming Language by Dennis M. Ritchie)

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

 

Answer: B

The key concept is that when a two-dimensional array is passed to a function in C, it is treated as a pointer to an array of rows.

The function parameter declaration must include the size of the inner dimension (number of columns) so the compiler can correctly perform pointer arithmetic to access elements. The number of rows is irrelevant because the function receives a pointer to the first row (which is a 1D array of a specific size), not the entire block of memory as a single object. 

Internally, the compiler converts all three valid function declarations shown :

  • void fun(char (*a)[4], int size);
  • void fun(char a[][4], int size);
  • void fun(char a[3][4], int size);

into the same internal representation: void fun(char (*a)[4], int size);, which is a function that accepts a pointer to a 1D array of 4 characters. 

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

B is the right answer

strcollection + 1 points to the next element of the array. The displacement (no. of bytes to move forward) depends on the “elements” of the array which are addresses.

 

The size of addresses in the system is 4B. So strcollection + 1 = 1000 + 4

 

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Without parentheses, +1 jumps over one single pointer slot; with parentheses, +1  jumps over the entire array block.

If there are no parentheses (Type *arr[N]), +1 treats the name as an array of address slots and jumps by exactly 1 × Size of a Pointer; whereas if there are parentheses (Type (*ptr)[N]), +1 treats it as a pointer to a collective block and jumps by the size of the whole container, which is calculated as 1 × N × Size of type (Base address+ sizeof(type).

Prerequisite DSA: QUICK WAY

This function is an in-order print traversal of a Binary Search Tree (BST) generated by a binary search breakdown.

Instead of tracing every single recursive stack frame manually, you can draw the tree structure directly to get the answer

Function structure: 

  1. Find midpoint m = (a + b) / 2
  2. Print m or process m
  3. Recursive call on left half (a, m - 1)
  4. Recursive call on right half (m + 1, b)

This is exactly how a Binary Search Tree splits intervals. The node is processed before its children (Pre-order printing).

Step 1: Build the Midpoint Tree for Range (0, 6)

  • Root: Midpoint of (0, 6) is (0+6)/2 = 3
  • Left Child: Midpoint of left remaining range (0, 2) is (0+2)/2 = 1
  • Right Child: Midpoint of right remaining range (4, 6) is (4+6)/2 = 5

Continue splitting down to the individual leaf nodes:

  • Left of 1 is range (0, 0) \rightarrow 0
  • Right of 1 is range (2, 2) \rightarrow 2
  • Left of 5 is range (4, 4) \rightarrow 4
  • Right of 5 is range (6, 6) \rightarrow 6

       3
     /   \
    1     5
   / \   / \
  0   2 4   6

Step 2: Read it based on printf placement

Look at where the printf statement sits relative to the recursive calls:

  • Since printf("%d", m); is executed before both recursive steps, it is a Pre-order Traversal (Root \rightarrow Left \rightarrow Right).

Simply read your drawn tree from top to bottom, left to right in pre-order sequence:

  • Output: 3102546

🧠 Quick Formula Summary

  • If printf is at the top \rightarrow Read Pre-order: 3 1 0 2 5 4 6
  • If printf is in the middle \rightarrow Read In-order: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6
  • If printf is at the bottom \rightarrow Read Post-order: 0 2 1 4 6 5 3

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_point#Sequence_points_in_C_and_C++

Before a function is entered in a function call. The order in which the arguments are evaluated is not specified, but this sequence point means that all of their side effects are complete before the function is entered. In the expression f(i++) + g(j++) + h(k++), f is called with a parameter of the original value of i, but i is incremented before entering the body of f. Similarly, j and k are updated before entering g and h respectively. However, it is not specified in which order f(), g(), h() are executed, nor in which order i, j, k are incremented. If the body of f accesses the variables j and k, it might find both, neither, or just one of them to have been incremented. (The function call f(a,b,c) is not a use of the comma operator; the order of evaluation for a, b, and c is unspecified.)

questions.html:
Mark all options which are likely to create problems with memory, i.e., run time error or has a memory leak.

Assume that malloc is successful in all cases.

Program 1:
int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
*p = 0;
free(p);
*p = 0;

Program2:
int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
*p = 0;
free(p);
p = 0;

Program 3:
int *p = malloc(3*sizeof(int));
*p = 0;
p++;
free(p);

Program 4:
int *p = malloc(sizeof(char));
*p = 0;
questions.solution:
Answer: A, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 18)

Answer: A, C, D

Program 1:

int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
*p = 0;
free(p);
*p = 0;

Line 1 is valid, so is line 2 where the value of that heap memory is altered, and line 3 where the memory is freed.

Writing into the freed memory is illegal: Dangling Pointer

Program 2:

int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
*p = 0;
free(p);
p = 0;

It’s same as Program 1 till line 3. In line 4 however notice that the pointer is instructed to point to different memory location (0 in case of pointer is NULL)[1].

The value of pointer is changed not the value at memory location pointed by the pointer. This would be illegal if the reference to heap allocated memory was lost but since it was already freed this is legal.

Program 3: 

int *p = malloc(3*sizeof(int));
*p = 0;
p++;
free(p);

Line 1, 2 are legal, and asks for 3 int memory locations. In line 3 the pointer is pointing to the second (1th) int and is then freed, but the the first (0th) int is never freed: Memory leak

Program 4: 

int *p = malloc(sizeof(char));
*p = 0;

Asked for 1 byte (sizeof(char)) and using as int: Writing to an area which is not your own, illegal.

 

 

 

References:

  1. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1296843/what-is-the-difference-between-null-0-and-0

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

The options that will create problems with memory are Program 1, Program 3, and Program 4.

Program 1: ❌ Problematic (Runtime Error)

  • The Issue: Dangling Pointer Dereference.
  • Why: After free(p); is executed, the memory block is released back to the heap. Line 5 (*p = 0;) tries to write data into that freed memory address, which causes undefined behavior or an immediate segmentation fault (runtime error).
Program 2: Perfect (Safe)
  • Why: free(p); releases the memory safely, and p = 0; resets the pointer to NULL. This prevents it from becoming a dangling pointer.
Program 3: ❌ Problematic (Runtime Error & Memory Leak)
  • The Issue: Invalid Free Pointer.
  • Understand: Executing p++ moves the pointer to point precisely to the second integer in that 3-integer block.
    • The heap block contains space for 3 integers, but because p is an int*, any pointer arithmetic operations scale by exactly one integer unit (4 bytes) at a time.
    • Assume Heap memory block starting at memory address 1000:
Memory Addresses:   [ 1000 ]    [ 1004 ]    [ 1008 ]
                    +----------+----------+----------+
Array Elements:     |  Int #1  |  Int #2  |  Int #3  |
                    +----------+----------+----------+
                      ▲          ▲
                      │          │
Initial state:     p (1000)      │
                                 │
After executing p++:          p (1004)
  •  Why this causes a Runtime Error on free(p)
    • The free() function relies on hidden metadata stored right before the allocated block (at address 996, for example) to know how many bytes to release.
    • Because p++ changed the pointer value to 1004, you are passing an address into free() that doesn't align with the start of an allocated block. The heap manager can't find its metadata, which triggers an immediate heap corruption runtime error.
  • Passing a modified pointer to free(p); breaks heap allocation rules, leading to a critical heap corruption crash (runtime error) and a permanent memory leak.
Program 4: ❌ Problematic (Buffer Overflow & Memory Leak)
  • The Issue: Heap Out-of-Bounds Write.
  • Why: malloc(sizeof(char)) allocates only 1 byte of memory. However, p is an integer pointer (int *p), so executing *p = 0; attempts to write an entire 4-byte integer into that 1-byte space. This overwrites adjacent heap metadata (buffer overflow crash). Additionally, the memory is never freed, creating a memory leak.
